\rev{Viewed as observable selection, LSTM--HaKAN implements a learned map $\bm\psi_k=E_\theta(\mathcal S_k)$ of the sampled history. Explicit delay coordinates retain selected samples with identifiable lags; $E_\theta$ instead mixes times, state variables, and past inputs into coordinates selected through the prediction loss. It is not constrained to reconstruct every historical sample, estimate the physical delay, or produce a one-to-one embedding. If two histories with different futures map to the same initial lift under the same future inputs, the subsequent deterministic predictor cannot distinguish them. Thus, learned history features can represent delayed dependence without enumerating its terms, but their predictive sufficiency must be evaluated rather than inferred from network capacity or window coverage.}

\rev{The Delay--RBF reference in Appendix~\ref{app:implementation} instantiates explicit selection: it appends the two delayed Lorenz coordinates or the three delayed separator coordinates at the known lag, then applies its prescribed nonlinear dictionary. This supplies a physically interpretable choice when the relevant variables and lags are known. During rollout it shifts a physical-state buffer and re-evaluates the dictionary using predicted states. DLM--K instead encodes the observed state--input window once; AFT subsequently reads the initial lift and predicted latent states, not newly observed delay coordinates. Its nonlinear correction is a learned closure, not a proof that $E_\theta$ spans an invariant subspace. Known delayed coordinates could also be combined with learned features, but this would require a separately fitted and validated model; the present comparison establishes no universal preference between explicit and learned history representations.}
